findings.title: Local cache entry is written before the DB write, letting devices bypass the limit
findings.body: In `tagDeviceUI` the cache key is stored (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. Now that `TagDevice` propagates the store error (impl.go:147) and `Anonymous.Authenticate` rejects the request on `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the first request from an over-limit device fails, but the cache entry is already present. Every subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL short-circuits at the cache check and returns nil, so the device is authenticated anonymously and never recorded. The configured device limit is therefore trivially bypassed by retrying the request, and transient DB errors are also "cached" as success.

findings.title: Count-then-insert is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads the device count with `CountDevices` and then performs the upsert in a separate session. Concurrent anonymous requests (and multiple Grafana instances sharing a DB) can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then each insert a new row, so the number of anon devices can exceed the configured limit by the number of concurrent requests. If the limit is meant as a hard cap (e.g. for licensing/billing), this check needs to be done inside a transaction or enforced by a conditional insert.

findings.title: updateDevice reports ErrDeviceLimitReached when the UPDATE matched but changed nothing
findings.body: `updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected` for an UPDATE returns the number of *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set). Since MySQL DATETIME columns have second precision, an existing, known device that re-tags within the same second with the same client IP and user agent produces 0 changed rows and will be wrongly rejected with "device limit reached", denying anonymous access to a device that is already counted. The condition conflates "row not found" with "nothing changed".

findings.title: Raw error returned from Authenticate yields an opaque 5xx instead of a proper status/message
findings.body: `Anonymous.Authenticate` returns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which is a plain `fmt.Errorf` value. Other authn clients return `errutil`-based errors so the HTTP layer can produce a correct status code (e.g. 401/403/429) and a stable messageId. As written, a user hitting the device limit will get a generic internal-error response (and the error will be logged as an unexpected failure) rather than a meaningful "too many anonymous devices" response, making the feature hard to diagnose and inconsistent with the rest of authn.

findings.title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips per anonymous request
findings.body: The previous implementation tagged the device in a background goroutine with its own timeout; now `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` runs inline during authentication. For every cache miss (cache TTL is 29 min, and the cache is per-instance) this executes a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` plus an upsert before the request can proceed, so anonymous page loads now block on DB latency and the count scan grows with the number of stored devices. On a busy anonymous instance (or after a restart, when the cache is empty) this can noticeably increase request latency and DB load.

findings.title: New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is undocumented
findings.body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read from `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the option is not added to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or the configure-grafana documentation. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its default (0 = unlimited), or that reaching the limit blocks new anonymous devices from authenticating.

findings.title: No test for the main intended behaviour: updating an already-known device when the limit is reached
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device is rejected once the limit is reached. The core of the feature — that an existing device (one already counted) can still be refreshed via `updateDevice` and does not get `ErrDeviceLimitReached` — is untested, as is the behaviour for a device whose row exists but is older than `anonymousDeviceExpiration`. Given the `rowsAffected == 0` heuristic used in `updateDevice`, regressions here would silently lock out already-counted anonymous users.

findings.title: args slice is mutated inside the session callback, corrupting the query on retry
findings.body: Inside `updateDevice` the closure does `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`, mutating the captured outer `args` variable. `WithDbSession` can invoke the callback more than once (e.g. sqlite "database is locked" retries); on a second invocation the query string would be prepended again, producing `Exec(query, query, ...)` and a malformed statement/argument mismatch. Build the exec argument slice as a new local variable instead of reassigning the captured one.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit field is typed as `undefined`, not `number | undefined`
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the field type as `undefined`. The backend always sends a numeric `anonymousDeviceLimit` (no `omitempty` on the DTO), and the value is injected via `merge(this, defaults, options)` which bypasses type checking. Consumers reading `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` will see the type `undefined` and cannot compare it to a number without a cast. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` to match `GrafanaConfig`.
